title: Hands-On Problem Solving
keyIdea: Maths tools help you think. Fingers are quick for small sums, but you only have 10. A ten frame holds 10 counters in two rows of 5, so you can see a full ten at a glance and then the extra ones. Cube towers stand side by side, so you can see which number is more and how many more. Pick the tool that fits the job, use it to work out the answer, and use it again to check.
familyTip: Keep a cup of 20 buttons or pasta shapes and an egg box cut down to 10 holes as a home ten frame. When a sum comes up, ask: fingers, ten frame or towers? Then ask why. Let your child show you the answer with the tool, and use it to check your answers too, especially when you make a slip on purpose.

visual.caption: Which tool fits best? Drag each problem, or tap it and then a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: show sums on fingers, run out at 10 and fill a ten frame, snap rows into towers, pick the best tool, and check a friend.

kid: A tool helps you do maths. Your fingers are a tool. Counters, cubes and a ten frame are tools too.
Fingers are quick. To add 4 + 3, put up 4 fingers. Then put up 3 more. Count them all: 7. But you only have 10 fingers.
A ten frame has 10 boxes, in two rows of 5. Fill it up and you can see 10 at once. For 8 + 5, fill the frame. The 3 left over go in a new frame. That is 10 and 3: 13.

To see who has more, snap cubes into towers. Stand them side by side. The taller tower has more. Use a tool to check, too. A friend says 7 take away 3 is 5. Put out 7 counters and take 3 away. 4 are left, so the friend made a slip.
adult: Ages 5 to 6. This matches the EYFS early learning goal for Number, the Year 1 National Curriculum aim to solve one-step problems using concrete objects and pictorial representations, and CCSS K.OA.A.2: solve addition and subtraction problems within 10 by using objects or drawings. Choosing a representation, not just using one, is the skill being built.

The lab has five tasks. Children show two sums on fingers, find that 8 + 5 runs out of fingers and fill two ten frames instead, snap a spread-out row and a bunched row into cube towers to compare 6 and 9, pick the best tool for three problems with a reason, and check two friends' take-away answers with counters.

Common mistakes. Children think a longer, spread-out row has more (a conservation slip), count from 1 again instead of seeing the full ten, or answer 'how many more?' by adding the two numbers. Some see fingers as cheating; they are a fine tool that simply stops at 10. Ask 'why did you pick that tool?' as often as 'what is the answer?'.

practice.prompt: 7 + 6. Can you show it on your fingers?
practice.hint: Count your fingers. How many do you have? Is 7 + 6 more than that?
practice.explain: You have 10 fingers. 7 + 6 = 13, which is more than 10. Use a ten frame instead.

practice.prompt: A ten frame has {a} counters in it. How many empty boxes are there?
practice.hint: A ten frame has 10 boxes. Count the empty ones, or work out 10 take away the full ones.
practice.explain: 10 boxes, {a} are full, so 10 − {a} = {=10-a} are empty.

practice.prompt: Row A has 4 counters spread far apart. Row B has 6 counters close together. Which has more?
practice.hint: Spread out does not mean more. Snap each row into a tower in your head.
practice.explain: Row B has 6, Row A has 4. 6 is more, even though Row A looks longer.

practice.prompt: One ten frame is full. The next ten frame has {b} counters. How many counters in all?
practice.hint: A full ten frame is 10. Then count on the counters in the next frame.
practice.explain: A full frame is 10, and {b} more makes 10 + {b} = {=10+b}.

practice.prompt: Tom builds a tower of {a} cubes. Kim builds a tower of {=a+d}. How many more cubes does Kim have?
practice.hint: Stand the towers side by side. Count only the cubes higher than Tom's tower.
practice.explain: Kim's tower is {=a+d} and Tom's is {a}. The extra cubes on top: {d} more.

pool.prompt: You are on a walk with no toys. What is 3 + 2?
choices: Wait to get a ten frame
pool.hint: Which maths tool do you always have with you?
pool.explain: Fingers are always with you. Put up 3, then 2 more: 5.

pool.prompt: You fill one ten frame and have {b} counters left over. How many counters in all?
pool.hint: A full ten frame is 10. Add the left-over counters.

pool.prompt: Which tool is best to see who has more, 6 or 9?
pool.hint: You want to compare two numbers side by side.
pool.explain: Two towers side by side show 9 is taller. The extra 3 cubes show 3 more.

pool.prompt: Put out {a} counters. Take away {b}. How many are left?
pool.hint: Take away the counters one at a time, then count what is left.

pool.prompt: Why use a ten frame for 8 + 5?
choices: You can see the full 10, then 3 more
pool.hint: What does a full ten frame show you at a glance?
pool.explain: 8 + 5 is more than 10 fingers. A full frame shows 10 at once, then 3 more: 13.

pool.prompt: Ben says 9 take away 4 is 6. He checks with counters. What does he find?
choices: 6 are left, so he is right
pool.hint: Picture 9 counters. Take 4 away. Count what is left.
pool.explain: 9 take away 4 leaves 5 counters. Ben said 6, so the counters show his slip.

pool.prompt: Tom has 5 cubes. Kim has 8. Ana says Kim has 13 more. What did Ana do?
choices: She added them; it is 3 more
pool.hint: How many more means the extra cubes on the taller tower.
pool.explain: 5 + 8 = 13 is adding. Side by side, Kim's tower is 3 cubes taller: 3 more.

pool.prompt: A ten frame is full. How many counters are in it?
pool.hint: A ten frame has two rows of 5 boxes.
pool.explain: Two rows of 5 is 10, so a full ten frame holds 10 counters.
